question:
Patient note:
A 70-year-old man was referred from primary care to the renal-medicine clinic for progressive azotemia identified on routine laboratory monitoring; he arrived accompanied by his spouse and was able to provide a coherent, detailed history without prompting. He reports that type 2 diabetes mellitus was diagnosed at age 48 after an employment physical revealed a fasting plasma glucose of 168 mg/dL, and over the ensuing two decades he has escalated from diet and metformin to a multi-dose basal–bolus insulin regimen. Approximately eight years ago ophthalmology documented multiple microaneurysms with focal laser photocoagulation to the right eye, and podiatry follows him for distal symmetric sensorimotor neuropathy manifesting as diminished vibration and occasional burning discomfort in the forefeet for which he takes nightly gabapentin; despite these issues he remains fully independent in activities of daily living. Three years prior to today’s visit he was admitted elsewhere for sudden-onset right-sided facial droop and slurred speech that resolved within 36 hours; brain MRI at that time demonstrated a small left pontine diffusion-positive lesion consistent with an acute lacunar infarct, and subsequent carotid duplex studies and cardiac telemetry failed to identify a high-risk embolic source. He completed six weeks of outpatient speech therapy and has had no further neurologic events, no residual limb weakness, and denies episodes of transient monocular blindness, transient aphasia, or focal sensory loss. He has never experienced crushing substernal pain, diaphoresis with exertion, emergency catheterization, or hospital admission for fluid overload; a resting transthoracic echocardiogram performed last winter in the course of pre-operative clearance for cataract surgery showed a left-ventricular ejection fraction of 62 % with no regional wall-motion abnormalities, normal chamber sizes, and trivial tricuspid regurgitation. He walks his dog briskly for 20 minutes twice daily without chest discomfort or calf cramping, and distal pulses have been described as palpable and symmetric during podiatry examinations. He has no chronic cough, wheeze, orthopnea, or requirement for inhalers, has never been intubated, and chest imaging obtained within the past year for a pulmonary nodule screening protocol was unremarkable apart from mild age-related basilar atelectasis. He denies dyspepsia, hematemesis, melena, or prior endoscopic findings of gastric or duodenal ulceration. He does not consume alcohol, has never used intravenous drugs, and tested negative for hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody during a life insurance evaluation five years ago; liver chemistry panels have consistently revealed aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, bilirubin, and international normalized ratio within reference limits, and abdominal ultrasound last month showed a smooth hepatic contour without ascites or focal lesions. There is no personal history of hematologic or solid malignancy, lymphadenopathy, cytopenias, or constitutional “B” symptoms. Surgical history includes only bilateral cataract extraction and an appendectomy in early adulthood. Current medications are insulin glargine 32 units nightly, insulin lispro dosed with meals per sliding scale, lisinopril 20 mg daily, chlorthalidone 12.5 mg daily for long-standing hypertension, low-dose aspirin 81 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, gabapentin 300 mg at bedtime, and over-the-counter vitamin D3; he takes no non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, proton-pump inhibitors, or corticosteroids. Vital signs in clinic show temperature 36.8 °C, blood pressure 134/76 mm Hg seated in the right arm, heart rate 78 beats per minute regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 % breathing ambient air; body-mass index is 28 kg/m². He appears well nourished, conversant, and in no distress. Cardiovascular examination reveals normal jugular venous pulsation, a regular rhythm with crisp S1 and S2, and no murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Lungs are clear to auscultation throughout with good air entry and no wheezes or crackles. The abdomen is soft, non-tender, and without organomegaly or bruits; there are no stigmata of chronic liver disease. Neurologic testing demonstrates intact cranial nerves, full strength in all limbs, normal coordination, and a steady gait; plantar responses are flexor, and sensation to pinprick is reduced below the ankles symmetrically. Peripheral pulses are 2+ at the radial, femoral, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis arteries bilaterally, and there is no lower-extremity edema or trophic skin change. Laboratory data obtained this morning reveal hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL, white blood cell count 6.2 × 10⁹/L, platelets 232 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.8 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 22 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 48 mg/dL, serum creatinine 2.3 mg/dL (baseline 2.1–2.4 over the past six months) with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 28 mL/min/1.73 m², fasting glucose 142 mg/dL, HbA1c 7.2 %, calcium 8.7 mg/dL, phosphate 4.2 mg/dL, AST 24 U/L, ALT 21 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 78 U/L, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, albumin 3.9 g/dL, and an LDL cholesterol of 74 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows 2+ protein, negative blood, and no cellular casts; a spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio measured last week was 1,220 mg/g. An electrocardiogram performed in the clinic depicts normal sinus rhythm at 76 beats per minute, normal axis, and no Q waves, ST-segment deviation, or significant repolarization abnormality. A recent non-contrast CT of the head reviewed today confirms a chronic pontine lacune without new parenchymal changes. The patient seeks guidance regarding further evaluation and management of his declining renal function in the context of long-standing diabetes complicated by eye and nerve involvement, and he wishes to understand anticipated progression and timing of potential renal replacement therapy while maintaining his current active lifestyle.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index adds age points to weighted comorbidity points:
• Age 70 (70–79): 3.
• Diabetes with end-organ damage, documented by retinopathy requiring laser therapy and peripheral neuropathy: 2. Do not also score uncomplicated diabetes.
• Moderate-to-severe chronic kidney disease: persistent renal impairment with eGFR 28 mL/min/1.73 m² (stage 4): 2.
• Cerebrovascular disease: MRI-confirmed prior pontine infarct: 1. No residual hemiplegia to score.
• No other qualifying comorbidity is documented. Hypertension does not add points.
Total = 3 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 8.
Final answer: 8
